A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SoS hierarchy is polynomially efficient for degree-d polynomials, and polynomially efficient even for sparse polynomials, but polynomially inefficient for general polynomials.
we show that SoS can be used as a black-box for polynomial optimization, and that the approximation ratio improves as the level of relaxation increases, albeit at the expense of more variables.

we give a polynomial-time algorithm for the following task: given a polynomial f with n variables and degree d, compute a unit direction x in R{\String^}n such that the value abs(f(x)) is at most (1+τ) times the optimum of the d-level SoS SDP for f.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of SoS is not monotonic in the level q.
the SoS hierarchy is capable of solving polynomial optimization problems in the regime of n << q, where it has been previously thought that SoS is incapable of solving such problems.
the SoS hierarchy can be a useful tool for polynomial optimization, even in the regime where the degree is large relative to the dimension.
